text: Before entering a trade, write down the setup, invalidation level, and exit conditions. A plan is useful only if you can follow it.
A stop-loss is a risk-control tool, not a guarantee against slippage or gaps. Understand the product and order type.
Keep a trading journal: record the setup, reasoning, risk, and lesson learned.
Missing a move is not a failure. Avoid chasing price; protecting your decision process matters more than catching every move.
After a frustrating result, pause and review your rules before making another decision. Avoid revenge trading.
Confidence should come from a repeatable process and honest records, not from one winning trade.
Notice emotional triggers such as FOMO, impatience, and overconfidence. Naming a trigger can help you slow down.
Support and resistance are zones, not perfectly precise lines. Watch how price behaves around an area.
A moving average summarizes past prices; it does not predict the future. Signals can be noisy in sideways markets.
Volume can add context to price moves, but data quality and meaning vary across markets and venues.
RSI is not a standalone buy or sell signal. Consider context, trend, timeframe, and tested rules.
A breakout can fail and return to its prior range. Define what would invalidate the idea.
Understand fees, spreads, liquidity, and slippage. Costs can materially affect frequent trading.
Consistency includes following the rule to sit out when conditions are unclear.
A chart pattern can look different across timeframes. Define your primary timeframe before interpreting signals.
